claude_take: The boldest claim in AI today is also the least verified: OpenAI says its models disproved a 27-year-old theorem, resting entirely on the company's own word until outside mathematicians finish checking it, while Anthropic's much quieter news, six drug companies now running real pipelines on Claude, earned a fraction of the attention despite already having something to show for it. That same asymmetry shows up outside tech. Frasers Group never seized Hugo Boss in one dramatic move, it just kept buying shares until it crossed 50 percent, and Israel's electorate split so evenly that no result emerged at all. Accumulation beats the dramatic gesture most days; it's just a lot less fun to report.

items.headline: OpenAI Says Its AI System Disproved a 27-Year-Old Complexity Theory Conjecture
items.summary: OpenAI announced on October 26 that one of its internal models produced a proof disproving the Exponential Time Hypothesis, a foundational 1999 conjecture in computational complexity theory that hundreds of other papers have built on. The company published the result publicly along with a formal proof checked in the Lean theorem prover, and named an independent review panel, including the hypothesis's original authors and MIT's Ryan Williams, to examine whether it holds. Machine verification confirms the proof's internal logic but is not the same as full expert peer review, and OpenAI itself cautions the finding would not make hard computational problems practically easier to solve.

items.headline: Anthropic Reports Early Results From Six Drug-Discovery Partners Using Claude
items.summary: Anthropic said six partners, including Bristol Myers Squibb, Generate Biomedicines and BigHat Biosciences, are now using its Claude Science workbench in real drug-discovery work, alongside the company's own in-house program targeting neglected diseases. Partners reported early gains such as a shortened CAR-T genetic construct and large cuts in regulatory-documentation time, though the figures are self-reported and the work remains preclinical. It is a concrete step for a major AI lab moving from general-purpose assistants into specialized scientific tooling with named industry partners attached.

items.headline: Israel's Knesset Election Ends in a Historic Deadlock
items.summary: Israel's October 27 parliamentary election drew record turnout but produced no clear winner, with exit polls and early counts showing neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc nor opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot's bloc reaching the 61 seats needed for a majority. Arab parties made their strongest-ever showing, but Eisenkot has ruled out governing with them or sharing power with Netanyahu, raising the prospect of prolonged coalition talks or a repeat election in Israel's first vote since the October 7, 2023 attacks.

items.headline: Share of Americans Using AI Chatbots Nearly Daily More Than Doubled in Five Months
items.summary: New Epoch AI and Ipsos polling found the share of US adults using AI chatbots on at least six days a week rose from about 8 percent in March 2026 to 19 percent in August, even as overall use climbed more modestly. A separate Pew Research survey the same month found most Americans who have never used a chatbot still have no plans to start. Together the data describes a splitting public: a hardening core of daily users pulling away from a majority that remains occasional or entirely unengaged.

items.headline: Frasers Group Takes Majority Control of Hugo Boss
items.summary: Mike Ashley's Frasers Group has crossed the 50 percent ownership threshold in Hugo Boss after buying a further stake for about 7.6 million euros, making the German fashion house a Frasers subsidiary whose results will be folded into Frasers' own accounts. The move caps a yearlong campaign that began with a rejected takeover bid and installed Frasers chief executive Michael Murray as Hugo Boss's board chair in September, though German minority-shareholder protections still limit how much day-to-day control Frasers can exert over the roughly 49 percent of the company still in other hands.

items.headline: Karl Popper's Falsifiability
items.headline_fr: Le critère de falsifiabilité de Karl Popper
items.summary: Karl Popper argued that what separates genuine science from pseudo-science is not that a theory can be confirmed by evidence, but that it can, in principle, be proven wrong. A theory earns scientific standing only by making risky predictions that a single contrary observation could refute; one flexible enough to explain away any possible result tells us nothing at all. The idea reshaped how researchers design experiments, and it still underlies today's debates over which claims in AI, medicine, and economics are genuinely testable rather than merely unfalsifiable hype.
items.summary_fr: Karl Popper soutenait que ce qui distingue une véritable démarche scientifique d'une pseudo-science n'est pas la possibilité de confirmer une théorie par des preuves, mais bien la possibilité, en principe, de la réfuter. Une théorie n'acquiert un statut scientifique qu'en formulant des prédictions risquées qu'une seule observation contraire pourrait invalider ; une théorie assez souple pour expliquer n'importe quel résultat ne nous apprend en réalité rien. Cette idée a transformé la façon de concevoir les expériences scientifiques et alimente encore aujourd'hui les débats sur ce qui, en intelligence artificielle, en médecine ou en économie, relève d'une affirmation vérifiable plutôt que d'un simple battage non falsifiable.
